cards.front: Which entry point works directly across the files of a local code repository?
cards.back: Claude Code (the terminal tool) reads, edits, and runs code in your repo. Use claude.ai chat for quick Q&A, Projects for reusable context, and the API to build automation.

cards.front: When should you use a Claude Project instead of a plain chat?
cards.back: When you reuse the same instructions and reference material across many chats. A Project's custom instructions and knowledge sources apply to every conversation in it.

cards.front: When is the API the right entry point?
cards.back: When you need Claude embedded in your own software, running programmatically with no person in the loop.

cards.front: Which model for the hardest, multi-step reasoning?
cards.back: Claude Opus 4.8 — the most capable model. Reserve it for genuinely complex work where accuracy outweighs cost and speed.

cards.front: Which model for high-volume, balanced work?
cards.back: Claude Sonnet 5 — strong quality at a cost and speed that scale.

cards.front: Which model for simple, fast, high-volume tasks?
cards.back: Claude Haiku 4.5 — the lowest latency and cost for lightweight tasks like classification or language detection.

cards.front: What feature helps Claude reason through multi-step problems?
cards.back: Extended (adaptive) thinking — it lets Claude work through intermediate steps before answering.

cards.front: How do you get accurate answers about events after the training cutoff?
cards.back: Enable web search so Claude can retrieve current information; reasoning alone cannot recover facts it never learned.

cards.front: Your long chat is dragging in irrelevant earlier details. What is the fix?
cards.back: Start a fresh conversation focused on the current topic; everything earlier is context Claude may draw on.

cards.front: Why not run every task on the biggest model?
cards.back: Match the model to the task. Simple/high-volume work runs well on Haiku or Sonnet; Opus is for the hardest reasoning. Oversizing wastes cost and latency.

cards.front: What are the core elements of a well-structured prompt?
cards.back: Role, a clear task, relevant context, the desired output format, and examples.

cards.front: Instructions keep missing a specific format. What works better?
cards.back: Show two or three worked input-to-output examples (few-shot). Demonstrating the pattern beats describing it.

cards.front: Why change only one thing at a time when iterating?
cards.back: So you can tell which change caused the effect; changing many at once makes the result uninterpretable.

cards.front: Best fix for a vague, off-target answer?
cards.back: Be specific — state the exact scope, format, and success criteria.

cards.front: A complex request returns shallow results. What helps?
cards.back: Decompose it into focused steps; do and check each before it feeds the next.

cards.front: 'Don't be so formal' is not working. Better approach?
cards.back: Positively describe the tone you do want (warm, conversational) with a short example. Say what to do, not just what to avoid.

cards.front: Claude does not know your internal policy. What is essential?
cards.back: Provide the policy text as context; capability cannot substitute for a document it never saw.

cards.front: When are few-shot examples worth adding?
cards.back: When a task has a specific format or edge cases that plain instructions keep getting wrong. For simple tasks Claude already handles, skip them.

cards.front: Does confident, fluent writing mean the answer is correct?
cards.back: No — Claude can be confidently and articulately wrong. Fluency is not a reliability signal.

cards.front: Claude cites a study or statistic. What must you do before publishing?
cards.back: Independently verify the claim and that the cited source actually says it; citations can be fabricated.

cards.front: A citation looks authoritative but you cannot find the source anywhere. Likely cause?
cards.back: A hallucination — a plausible-looking but nonexistent citation. Treat it as unverified.

cards.front: Which outputs require human verification?
cards.back: High-stakes, factual, legal/medical, or irreversible ones. Validate before you act or put your name on it.

cards.front: A real, working citation URL — is the claim now proven?
cards.back: No — confirm the linked source actually supports the specific claim, not just that the page exists.

cards.front: How much verification does an output need?
cards.back: Scale it with stakes and reversibility. Brainstorming needs little; a tax figure or contract needs independent human review.

cards.front: Claude's resume shortlist skews to one demographic. Response?
cards.back: Treat it as a possible bias signal — examine the criteria and keep human oversight.

cards.front: Who is accountable for Claude's output you send under your name?
cards.back: You are. Validate the facts and reasoning first.

cards.front: Which steps are best to delegate to Claude?
cards.back: Well-specified, repeatable, checkable, low-risk steps. Keep ambiguous, high-stakes, accountability-bearing judgment with a human.

cards.front: What decides whether an action can be automated vs. needs human approval?
cards.back: The cost and reversibility of an error. Cheap and reversible can auto-proceed; costly or irreversible needs human review.

cards.front: How do you describe a Claude workflow's value to stakeholders?
cards.back: Honestly — pair the real benefit with the limitations and where humans stay in the loop. Do not overpromise.

cards.front: Moving from 'I use Claude' to 'our workflow uses Claude'?
cards.back: Capture working prompts, context, and configuration in a shared, reusable setup so the whole team gets consistent results.

cards.front: Best first process to automate with Claude?
cards.back: A frequent, well-defined, low-risk task with clear inputs and checkable outputs.

cards.front: Who should hold accountability for a final decision in an AI-assisted workflow?
cards.back: A designated human owner who reviews and approves. A tool cannot be accountable.

cards.front: Your workflow only lives in your head. What is the risk?
cards.back: It is fragile. Document steps, prompts, and config so others can run it when you are away.

cards.front: What do a Project's custom instructions do?
cards.back: They apply automatically to every chat in the Project — standing rules for tone, format, and behavior.

cards.front: Where should reusable reference documents go in a Project?
cards.back: As knowledge sources. Tone and format rules go in custom instructions.

cards.front: Claude keeps quoting last year's prices. Root-cause fix?
cards.back: Update the Project's knowledge source to current data. Stale config is a top failure cause.

cards.front: Main advantage of Project context over per-prompt context?
cards.back: Every chat in the Project inherits it, raising quality and consistency across all of them.

cards.front: Two unrelated kinds of work — one Project or two?
cards.back: Two. Separate Projects keep each set of instructions and knowledge focused and relevant.

cards.front: How do you keep Project knowledge trustworthy over time?
cards.back: Review and refresh it on a regular cadence; Claude will not update your sources for you.

cards.front: Conflicting policy versions in a Project's knowledge. Fix?
cards.back: Keep only the current authoritative version; remove outdated and draft copies so Claude cites the right one.

cards.front: About to paste a config with a live API key. What do you do?
cards.back: Redact or remove the secret first. Never paste live credentials; asking Claude to 'ignore' it does not undo the exposure.

cards.front: Before using regulated personal data (PII/PHI) in a tool?
cards.back: Follow your data policy and get authorization; minimize or anonymize what you do not need.

cards.front: Most important thing to know before entering sensitive data?
cards.back: Where the data goes, how it may be used or retained, and whether policy permits it.

cards.front: Confidential doc plus an unapproved tool. Right move?
cards.back: Do not. Use only tools approved for that data class; deleting the chat later does not undo the exposure.

cards.front: What is data minimization?
cards.back: Include only the data the task requires, and no more, to reduce exposure of sensitive info.

cards.front: Why does data classification matter before pasting?
cards.back: It sets the handling rules — some classes may not be entered into certain tools at all.

cards.front: Employee uses a personal, unvetted AI account for company data. Concern?
cards.back: Company data flows outside approved controls and agreements — a core governance risk.

cards.front: Before sending Claude output to an external partner?
cards.back: Review it to ensure no confidential or personal internal data was carried into the output.

cards.front: Answers are generic and could fit any company. Root cause?
cards.back: A context-poor prompt. Add the specific details of your situation.

cards.front: You described the format three times and it is still wrong. Durable fix?
cards.back: Provide a concrete example of the exact output you want.

cards.front: Simple high-volume job is slow/costly on the biggest model. Fix?
cards.back: Switch to a smaller, faster model suited to the task.

cards.front: Same manual correction every day. Durable fix?
cards.back: Encode it once in the Project's custom instructions instead of patching each chat.

cards.front: Answer is confidently out of date on a recent topic. Fix?
cards.back: Enable web search — the gap is the training cutoff, not reasoning.

cards.front: An output regressed after you changed several things at once. Move?
cards.back: Revert and reintroduce changes one at a time to isolate the cause.

cards.front: What is a sound troubleshooting sequence?
cards.back: Diagnose the root cause — ambiguous ask, missing context, wrong model, or wrong entry point — then fix that specific cause durably.
